The term a cappella is Italian for “in the manner of the chapel.” It was used in reference to church music, which would be performed without instrumental accompaniment. A cappella singing can be traced back to the 13th century, when composers such as Philippe de Vitry wrote secular choral music. The style was popular throughout Europe and even in England, where Henry VIII’s court musicians were known to perform a cappella. In the late 1800s, barbershop quartets brought a cappella into the American mainstream.

The word estimable is defined as being worthy of respect or esteem. It comes from the Latin verb estimo, meaning to value highly. Estimate means to form an opinion about something, and estimator is a person who values things. An estimate is also a rough calculation of how much something will cost or how long it will take. The word estimate can be traced back to 1300-50; Middle English estimer, “to judge,” which in turn comes from Anglo-French estimer, “to esteem.” Estimable entered English in the early 16th century.

ACROSTIC — Today’s word is the acrostic. An acrostic is a poem in which the first letter of each line spells out a word or name. The acrostic has been around for thousands of years, and has been used by many different cultures. In fact, the very first acrostics were found on clay tablets dating back to 4000 BCE. They were written in cuneiform, an ancient form of writing that dates all the way back to the Sumerians. It was later adopted by the Akkadian, Elamite, Persian, Hittite, and Urartian civilizations. Each of these groups wrote in their own language, but they all used this ancient system of writing.

The minimum income needed to qualify for a mortgage varies by lender and location. What you earn is just one piece of the puzzle when applying for a loan, though. Lenders look at all of your monthly debts — such as car payments, student loans and credit card bills — plus living expenses like groceries and utilities. This includes rent or mortgage payments, insurance, taxes and maintenance.

The word onus has two meanings. One is a burden or responsibility, and the other is a tax or duty. Onus comes from the Latin onus, meaning “burden.” In English, we use onus to refer to both legal and moral responsibilities. The noun form of onus is onuses (plural). The adjective form is onerous, which means “burdensome” or “oppressive.” It also means “involving an obligation.” The adverbial form is onerously. Here are some examples of onus in a sentence.

Some believe that the word comes from the German word for quack, “quacksalber,” which refers to a person who is both an imposter and a doctor. The first known usage of the word in English was in Shakespeare’s King Lear, published in 1608. In the play, a foolish knight named Sir Andrew Aguecheek is described as being “most exquisitely quack-salved.” Quack-salving refers to a method of curing warts by using a special ointment called quacksalve. Soon after, the word quackery started appearing in print with its current meaning

The word inanity was coined by Samuel Johnson. It comes from Latin in-, “not,” and anus, meaning “wit.” So, literally, it means “without wit” or “lacking intelligence.” Inanity is not to be confused with insanity; that word means “madness,” not “stupidity.” Insanity implies some sort of mental illness, whereas inanity suggests a lack of common sense, a lack of basic understanding, a lack of awareness.

The Depuy-Dewitt House is one of the oldest houses in Albany NY. It was built by Dirck Van Dyke in 1724 as a wedding gift for his daughter, Elizabeth. She married Johannes DePuy, whose descendants occupied the house until 1937. The DePuys were early settlers who arrived from Holland around 1650. They became prosperous through their trading business with the Indians. In 1824, the house was sold to Charles Dewitt, son of General Lansing Dewitt. After several years of neglect, the house was rescued by the Historic Albany Foundation which has undertaken an extensive restoration. The house was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1971.

This week The Atlantic published an article about pedestrian deaths in the evening. According to the author, a new study from researchers at Carnegie Mellon University suggests that one of the reasons why more pedestrians are dying during nighttime hours is because of the way our eyes adapt to darkness. When you first walk out into the dark, your pupils will dilate and let in more light so you can see better. But if you’re wearing sunglasses when walking in the dark, your pupils won’t get as big, which means you won’t be able to see as well. As a result, drivers may not be able to see you, and that could lead to accidents.

What do we mean by the term “conservative”? The word itself has become so politically charged that it is almost useless to use, but it’s worth thinking about what we actually mean when we say someone is a conservative. I think we should understand being a conservative as being a person who believes in and seeks to preserve the traditional ways of living of his society. This may be thought of as a kind of instinctive attachment to one’s culture. Conservatives are not necessarily against change, but they tend to distrust radical changes and seek to preserve those things that make up the essence of their culture.

The consumer price index rose 0.4% from a month earlier, while the core measure, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was up 0.1%. Compared with a year ago, CPI rose 1.3%, while the core rate was up 2.3%. For the past few years, the Fed has targeted annual inflation of around 2%, but it has undershot that level since early last year. A generation after the Civil Rights Act, the Reagan administration argued that Congress should repeal Title VII’s prohibition on disparate-impact claims because “the mere existence of a disparity is not in itself proof of discrimination.” The court’s conservative majority should be similarly skeptical about the arguments now being advanced by the Obama administration. They are arguments that would dramatically expand the reach and power of federal agencies. And they would do so by allowing regulators to interpret ambiguous statutes to create their own legal theories—without any congressional authorization.

Let’s consider a few recent examples of this phenomenon, which I’ll call the antidemocratic quest to save democracy from Trump. Last week, an activist federal judge in Seattle issued a nationwide restraining order barring the enforcement of key provisions of the president’s executive order on immigration. The ruling was based not on any constitutional or statutory challenge, but rather on the claim that it violated “the Constitution and laws of the United States” — a constitutional phrase that, as far as I can tell, is completely meaningless, since the Constitution contains no general prohibition against the government acting unfairly or unreasonably (and the courts have never recognized such a provision).

Charles Darwin was a man who liked to travel. He embarked on five major expeditions, and many smaller ones. His first adventure abroad took him to South America in 1831; he returned home five years later with his head full of new ideas. He visited Tenerife, Mauritius and New Zealand. But one of his favourite destinations was the island of Santiago, the largest of the Cape Verdes. Between 1832 and 1836 Darwin made three visits to this Portuguese colony. There is no doubt that the time spent there was critical to his development as a scientist. It was on Santiago that Darwin discovered his true vocation: he became an explorer of life itself.

In Isaac Asimov’s Foundation Trilogy, the social scientist Hari Seldon invented “psychohistory”: a blend of history, sociology and mathematical statistics that could predict the future. This was not magic but rather based on his theory that the actions of individuals might change but not the mass behavior of people in the aggregate. In other words, what happens to one person is unpredictable; what happens to a million people is quite predictable. Using this approach, he developed psychohistory to enable him to foresee the collapse of the Galactic Empire into thirty thousand years of darkness and barbarism and how to shorten this period to only a single millennium.

The word entreat has two meanings. The first is to beg, plead or beseech earnestly for something. The second meaning is to attempt to persuade someone to do something. The first definition is the most common usage of the word. Entreat comes from the Latin word intercedere which means to go between. In modern English, entreat is usually used in a negative context such as to entreat someone to stop doing something or not to do something. When used in this manner, it is often accompanied by the words please or don't. An example would be “Please, don’t talk about me like that!” This usage of entreat is similar to the phrase “please stop”.

It is a British term for what is known as an American-style crossword in the United States, although it has been used to describe cryptic crosswords elsewhere as well. In 2014, nine blue whales stranded on the California coast. The scientists analyzed the genetics of these whales to determine whether they were related and what their relationship was with other populations of blue whales. They found that three of the animals were likely mother and calf pairs. One of those pairs showed some inbreeding, but the other two did not. This is surprising since it’s thought that females do not mate until five years old and males do not mate until ten years old, so it would be expected that there would be more inbreeding among these whales than was observed.
